01.note: A man gave agents a bill of divorce for his wife and told them: if I do not come back within thirty days, let it be a divorce. He arrived at the end of the thirty days, but the ferry was on the far side of the river and he could not cross. He called out to the people on the other side: see that I have come, see that I have come. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as coming back.
01.why: The Gemara is testing Rava's view that a condition counts as unmet even when circumstances beyond the man's control caused it. It cites Shmuel's ruling as proof, then answers that a ferry delay is common enough that he should have stipulated for it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who rules that the man's shouting from across the river does not count as his return.

terms.meaning: The written document (in Hebrew, a get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it is written conditionally, to take effect only if he fails to return in time.
The boat used to cross the river. Because it was moored on the opposite bank, the man was stuck on the wrong side when his deadline ran out.

02.note: A man handed agents a bill of divorce for his wife, saying: if I do not return within thirty days, let it be a divorce. He reached the river at the end of the thirty days, but the ferry was on the other side and he could not cross in time. He shouted to the people across the river: see that I have come, see that I have come. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as a return.
02.why: The Gemara is asking whether a condition counts as unmet when the failure was beyond the man's control, such as illness. It cites Shmuel's ruling as evidence, then answers that a ferry being on the far bank is a common problem he should have stipulated for.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who rules that calling out from across the river is not a return, so the divorce stands.

terms.meaning: The written document (in Hebrew, a get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. This one was set to take effect only if he did not come back in time.

03.note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry into the family of Rav Haviva and began reciting the wedding blessing from the time of the betrothal, saying he was certain the family would not back out. The match fell through and they did back out. In a second short report, Rav Tahlifa from the Land of Israel came to Babylonia and recited six long wedding blessings; the Gemara says the law does not follow him.
03.why: The Gemara is asking from when the wedding-celebration blessing may be recited before the wedding. Rav Pappa began at betrothal because the wedding was already prepared; Ravina's case shows the risk of doing so.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A father who began the wedding blessing at his son's betrothal, sure the match would hold.

people.name: Rav Haviva
people.about: Head of the family Ravina's son was to marry into; that family later retracted.

people.name: Rav Tahlifa
people.about: A Sage from the West, meaning the Land of Israel, who came to Babylonia and recited six long blessings.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which legally binds the couple before the wedding itself; in this period it could still be called off by divorce.
The Babylonian Talmud's name for the Land of Israel, which lay west of Babylonia.

03.flag: Two unrelated short reports (Ravina's son's match, and Rav Tahlifa's six blessings) are joined in one story.

04.note: The young child of Rav Hiyya bar Abba, teacher of Reish Lakish's sons, died. Reish Lakish did not come on the first day; the next day he came with his spokesman, Yehuda bar Nahmani, and told him to say something about the child. Yehuda quoted verses saying God is angry at a sinful generation and its children die young, which the Gemara explains as telling Rav Hiyya he was important enough to be taken for the generation's sins. Reish Lakish then had him speak in praise of God, for the mourners, for those who comfort them, and for all Israel, and Yehuda closed each with a blessing.
04.why: The Gemara is asking how a mourners' blessing could be recited throughout the seven days of mourning; it answers that this happens when new visitors arrive, and cites this visit on the second day, with its series of blessings.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Teacher of Reish Lakish's son or sons; it is his child who died.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Comes to comfort his sons' teacher on the second day and directs his spokesman what to say.

people.name: Yehuda bar Nahmani
people.about: Reish Lakish's spokesman, who delivers the words of comfort and the blessings.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Comments that one should say 'many have drunk' but not 'many will drink', so as not to invite disaster.

people.name: Rav Hanan bar Rav
people.about: Explains a verse quoted in the comfort as a warning against speaking obscenely.

terms.meaning: A Sage's spokesman, who repeated and expanded the master's words aloud to a gathering.
A saying meaning one should not speak of possible future disasters, as if inviting them to happen.

05.note: A man came before Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said that he had slept with his bride and found no blood. She said she had been a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asked for the cloth from that night, had it soaked and washed, and found several drops of blood on it. He told the groom: go, take possession of your acquisition.
05.why: The Gemara is collecting cases where a groom claims his bride was not a virgin. Right after, Rav Ashi explains why Babylonian judges could not copy this washing test.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he examines the cloth and rules for the bride.

terms.meaning: The judge's way of saying the marriage stands as it was: the bride was a virgin and the groom has no claim against her.

06.note: A man came before Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said he had slept with his bride and found no blood; she said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel had two maidservants brought, one a virgin and one not, and seated each on the mouth of a wine barrel: the scent of the wine came from the mouth of the non-virgin but not from the virgin. He then seated the bride there, and no scent came from her. He told the groom: go, take possession of your acquisition.
06.why: It is one of a run of cases about a groom's claim that his bride was not a virgin. The Gemara then asks why he tested the maidservants first, and answers he had only heard of the method and would not shame a Jewish woman for nothing.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he tests the method on two maidservants before using it on the bride.

terms.meaning: The judge's way of saying the marriage stands: the bride is a virgin and the groom has no claim against her.

07.note: A man came before Rabban Gamliel the Elder and said that he had slept with his bride and found no blood. She said she came from the Dorketi family, whose women have neither menstrual blood nor the blood of virginity. Rabban Gamliel checked among her female relatives and found that she was telling the truth. He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition and called him fortunate to have married into the Dorketi family.
07.why: It continues a series of cases of grooms claiming their brides were not virgins. Afterward Rabbi Hanina says Rabban Gamliel's comfort was empty, since a woman without blood will have few children, and the Sages dispute what he actually said.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The judge who investigates the bride's family and confirms her claim.

terms.meaning: The name of the bride's family. The Gemara explains it as 'truncated generation'.
In Jewish law a woman who menstruates is forbidden to her husband for a time; a woman who never does avoids that issue.

08.note: In years of drought, a man came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said he had slept with his bride and found no blood; she said she was still a virgin. Rabbi saw that their faces were black from hunger. He had them taken to the bathhouse, fed and given drink, and then brought to a room; the groom slept with her again and found blood. Rabbi told him to take possession of his acquisition, and read over them the verse: their skin is shriveled upon their bones, it has become like a stick.
08.why: It is the last of a run of cases where a groom says his bride showed no sign of virginity, each showing a different reason the blood may be missing: here, famine. The chapter ends right after it.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he sees the couple are starving, has them fed, and rules for the bride.

terms.meaning: The judge's way of saying the marriage stands: the bride was a virgin and the groom has no claim against her.

09.note: Rav Aha used to put the bride on his shoulders and dance. The Sages asked him whether they could do the same. He told them: if a bride is like a wooden beam to you, fine; if not, no.
09.why: The Gemara is gathering accounts of Sages who danced to bring joy to a bride, such as Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai with a myrtle branch and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggling three branches.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: A Sage who danced with the bride on his shoulders.

terms.meaning: Rav Aha's test: only someone who feels no more stirred by the bride than by a piece of wood may carry her this way.

10.note: The Sages taught that a funeral procession turns aside to let a bride's procession pass, and both turn aside for a king of Israel. It was said of King Agrippa that he turned aside for a bride, and the Sages praised him.
10.why: Right after, the Gemara asks how the Sages could praise Agrippa when a king may not give up the honor due to him, and answers that it happened at a crossroads, where no one could tell he had yielded.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: A king who turned his entourage aside to let a bride's procession pass, and was praised for it.

11.note: A woman of great beauty had many men pressing to marry her, and she told them she was already betrothed. Later she went ahead and betrothed herself to a man. When the Sages asked her why, she explained that the first men were unworthy, so she claimed to be betrothed; now that worthy men had come, she accepted one. Rav Aha Sar HaBira raised this before the Sages at Usha, and they ruled that if she gives a reason for her first statement, she is believed.
11.why: The Gemara has taught that a woman who said she was married and then said she was not is believed if she gives a reason for her first claim. This incident is cited in support.

people.name: Rav Aha Sar HaBira
people.about: Brought this case before the Sages at Usha for a ruling.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, betrothal is the first, binding stage of marriage. A woman who is betrothed is forbidden to marry anyone else.
The town where the Sages gathered as a high court at the time.

12.note: Captive women were brought to Neharde'a to be ransomed, and Shmuel's father set guards over them. Shmuel asked who had guarded them until now; his father answered: if they were your daughters, would you treat them with such contempt? Later Shmuel's own daughters were taken captive and brought to the Land of Israel. They left their captors outside, went into Rabbi Hanina's study hall, each said 'I was taken captive, and I am pure', and were permitted. When the captors came in, Rabbi Hanina said these were daughters of great teachers, and it emerged that they were Shmuel's. He told Rav Shemen bar Abba, a priest, to marry one; Rav Shemen objected that there were witnesses overseas, and Rabbi Hanina said those witnesses were not before them.
12.why: The Gemara has taught that a captive woman who says she stayed pure is believed and may marry a priest, unless witnesses later testify she was violated. Rav Ashi reads Rabbi Hanina's reply about the overseas witnesses in that light.

people.name: Shmuel's father
people.about: Posted guards over the captive women at Neharde'a and rebuked his son's remark.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Questioned his father's guards; his own daughters were later taken captive.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Head of the study hall where Shmuel's daughters made their claim; he permitted them.

people.name: Rav Shemen bar Abba
people.about: A priest and relative of the daughters, told by Rabbi Hanina to marry one of them.

terms.meaning: Here it means she was not violated while in captivity. A captive woman is otherwise suspected of it and may not marry a priest.

terms.term: like an error that comes from the ruler
terms.meaning: A verse from Ecclesiastes, used here to say that the father's words came true, as if decreed: Shmuel's own daughters were later taken captive.

13.note: Shmuel told of a man who, chatting about something else, recalled being carried as a small child on his father's shoulder: they took him out of school, took off his shirt and immersed him so he could eat teruma that evening. Rabbi Hiyya added that the man said his friends kept away from him and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'. On the strength of this, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raised him to the priesthood.
13.why: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Hiyya could accept a brother's word that a man is a Levite when relatives may not testify. It answers that he meant a remark made in passing, and cites this case to show such remarks are trusted.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who reported this incident, as Rav Yehuda relates in his name.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Gives the end of the story, with the friends' nickname and the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who accepted the man as a priest on the basis of his remark.

people.name: Yohanan
people.about: The man in the story, whose friends nicknamed him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their households may eat, and only in a state of ritual purity.
Plural of halla, the portion of dough given to priests; like teruma, only priests may eat it.
Dipped in a ritual bath to become ritually pure.
Saying something in passing, in conversation about another matter, without any intent to testify. Such a remark is trusted more than a deliberate claim.

14.note: Rabbi Yosei the priest and Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav reported a case. A Jewish woman had been held as security for a debt in Ashkelon, and her family kept away from her, but her witnesses testified that she had not been alone with anyone or violated. The Sages told the family: if you believe the witnesses that she was held at all, believe them that she was not violated; if not, do not believe she was held.
14.why: Rav had said that when gentiles rule, even a woman jailed over money is forbidden to her husband. Rava objects with this case from gentile Ashkelon; the Gemara answers it is cited this way only because that is how it happened.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: One of the two Sages who testified about this case.

people.name: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav
people.about: The other Sage who testified about it.

terms.meaning: Held by gentiles as security for a debt. This raised the concern that she had been violated, which would forbid her to her husband.
The early code of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses. Rava quotes this case from the mishna's tractate Eduyyot.

15.note: A man rented his donkey to another and told him not to take the road along the Pekod River, where there was water, but the road through Neresh, where there was none. The renter took the Pekod road, and the donkey died. Before Rava, he admitted taking that road but claimed there was no water on it. Rava accepted his claim, reasoning that if he wanted to lie he could have said he took the Neresh road. Abaye told him this reasoning does not apply when there are witnesses against the claim.
15.why: Rav Ashi asks whether a woman who says she neither hid nor was violated is believed because she could have told a better lie. The Gemara compares this case, then notes that here water on the road was known for certain.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, who accepts the renter's claim.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects to Rava that the argument fails where witnesses contradict the claim.

terms.meaning: A legal argument: a claim is believed if the person could have won with an easier lie and did not use it. The Talmud calls this a miggo.

16.note: A man came to Mari bar Isak, or some say Hana bar Isak, from Bei Hoza'a, saying he was his brother and wanted his share of their father's property. Mari said he did not know him. Before Rav Hisda, the man was told to bring witnesses that he was the brother; he said he had them but they feared Mari, a violent man. Rav Hisda then told Mari to bring witnesses that the man was not his brother, and when Mari objected that the burden of proof is on the claimant, Rav Hisda said this is how he judges him and all violent men like him.
16.why: The Gemara has said that a maidservant may keep silent but would not also lie, since one does not commit two dishonest acts. It cites this case as proof: the frightened witnesses would hide the truth but would not testify falsely.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: A violent man who refused to recognize a man claiming to be his brother; some name him Hana bar Isak.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge, who put the burden of proof on Mari.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: From Genesis; cited by Rav Hisda as one whom his brothers did not recognize, since he left beardless and returned bearded.

terms.term: The burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: The usual rule: whoever wants to take property from another must prove his claim. Rav Hisda reverses it for a violent man.
A district far from the main Jewish towns of Babylonia, so the brother had been away a long time.

17.note: A betrothed man and woman who had divorced came before Rava over a money matter, while Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before him. Rava placed a go-between to keep them apart. Rav Adda objected that a divorce from betrothal allows direct payment; Rava answered that he could see these two were used to each other. In another version, Rava did not separate them, and it was Rav Adda who urged him to and gave the same reason.
17.why: A teaching says a priest who owes his divorced wife money must repay her through someone else, so they do not mix. Rav Nahman exempts a divorce from betrothal, since they are not used to each other; this case shows the exception failing.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge before whom the couple came.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: A Sage sitting before Rava, who debates with him about separating the couple.

terms.meaning: In the first, binding stage of marriage, before the wedding. This couple divorced at that stage.
One of the minor tractates of the Talmud, mainly about the laws of mourning, cited here for its teaching on a divorce from betrothal.

18.note: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said that he testified only once in his life, and on his testimony a slave was raised to the priesthood. The Gemara refuses to believe God would let a righteous man cause such a wrong, and emends: they sought to raise the slave on his word, but did not. He had seen teruma given to a slave in Rabbi Yosei's town, and testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's town.
18.why: The Gemara has explained that Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yosei's towns differed on whether eating teruma proves a man is a priest; this account shows that difference nearly making a slave a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Tells of the one time he testified, which nearly made a slave a priest.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their households, including their slaves, may eat.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the main early code of Jewish law.
Officially recognized as a priest, with the rights of lineage and marriage that come with it.

19.note: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing together when a man came up, bowed and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot. Rabbi Hanina asked what this was about. Rabbi Yonatan explained that the man had written his property over to his sons, and Rabbi Yonatan had forced them to feed him.
19.why: The Sages at Usha ruled that a man who gave his property to his son is still supported from it, and the Gemara asks if the law follows Rabbi Ile'a on this. The forcing implies the sons owed nothing by law, so it does not.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Was standing with Rabbi Yonatan and asked why the man kissed his foot.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: Had forced a man's sons to feed their father; the man thanked him by kissing his foot.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; here, the binding ruling on whether such sons must support their father.

20.note: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had a stepmother who was using up their father's money on her food. Rabbi Yohanan told them to have their father set aside land for her support. After the father died they went to Reish Lakish, who said that this only added to her support, and threatened that if they did not give her what she needed he would drive Rabbi Yohanan's ruling out of their ears. When they complained to Rabbi Yohanan, he said: what can I do? A man equal to me disagrees with me.
20.why: Right after, Rabbi Abbahu reports Rabbi Yohanan's own explanation: everything turns on the wording; land given 'for' her support adds to it, while land given 'as' her support fixes it.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Advised his relatives to have their father set aside land for his wife's support.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Ruled that the land only added to the widow's support, and pressed the sons hard to pay.

terms.meaning: The food and support a husband's estate owes his widow under her marriage contract.
